transcript.text: Just got a new Siemens dishwasher and there's always a bit of water left in the bottom under the filter after it finishes. Is it draining properly?

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. No, water remaining at the bottom of the tub indicates the dishwasher is not draining correctly. This suggests a blockage or pump issue despite the unit being new. This sounds like normal behaviour rather than a fault: A small amount of clean water around the filter or sump (a cup or so, under the filter level) is normal: it keeps the seals wet. It would be worth a closer look if dirty water above the filter, water covering the base, or water that smells. Take out the lower rack, then twist and lift out the filter in the bottom of the tub. Rinse it under the tap and clear any food, grease or glass from the sump underneath. Was the filter or sump blocked (and is it clean now), or was it already clean?
[Helpful to see: image "Where the filter is" — The filter sits in the base of the dishwasher, usually under the bottom spray arm. Twist it out anticlockwise and rinse it under a tap. Typical layout — your dishwasher may differ.]

Thanks, I've taken the filter out and it was already clean. The water is clean and only about a cupful, sitting in the sump under the filter, none in the main tub. It's the same the next day, not rising. Is that normal then?

No, it is not normal for a dishwasher to retain standing water after a cycle. This indicates a blockage in the drain hose or pump, or a fault with the drainage system. Is there standing water in the bottom, and is the drain pump silent or does it hum/buzz without clearing the water?

There's only that cupful of clean water in the sump under the filter, nothing in the main tub. I didn't notice any humming or buzzing from the pump, it seems quiet. Your last two answers contradict each other, so is it normal or not?

It is normal for a small amount of water to remain in the sump area under the filter after a cycle. This standing water helps keep the seals moist and prevents odours from escaping back into the kitchen. With the filter back in, close the door, choose cancel or a drain / rinse programme and let it run for a couple of minutes, listening near the bottom of the machine. Did the water pump away this time?

I haven't run that drain programme yet, so I can't say whether it pumped away. Going by your last answer, a cupful of clean water in the sump is normal for this machine, right? There's no error on the display, and it's cleaning and drying fine.

Before you start, switch it off and unplug it. Yes, it is normal for a small amount of water to remain in the sump under the filter after a cycle finishes. This residual water helps keep the seals lubricated and prevents odors from entering the pump area. With the filter out, bail out any water with a cup and sponge. There's a small pump cover in the sump — lift its clip and look underneath with a torch for glass, stones or bones, then gently turn the little impeller with a finger. Did you find something caught (and remove it), is the impeller broken, or does it turn freely with nothing there?
I haven't opened the pump cover and I'd rather not take apart a 2-week-old machine if I don't need to. Since you've said a cupful of clean water in the sump is normal, do I need to do that at all?

Yes, you should check the drain hose for kinks or blockages as this is a common cause of residual water in new dishwashers. If the hose is clear and the issue persists, contact Siemens support since the unit is only two weeks old. Is water leaking from the side of the door during washing, or has the machine stopped / gone into anti-flood with the drain pump running and water underneath rather than on the floor?

No, it hasn't stopped or shown any error, and it's cleaning and drying fine. I checked the drain hose and it's looped up under the sink with no kinks. So is the cupful of clean water in the sump normal or not? I've had conflicting answers.

Yes, a small amount of standing water in the sump under the filter is normal for most dishwashers. This water acts as a seal to prevent drain odours from entering the machine and does not indicate a fault. Under the sink, look where the drain hose joins the waste. On a newly fitted sink waste the little blanking plug inside the spigot has to be cut out, and the sink trap mustn't be blocked — run the sink tap and check it drains freely. Was the blanking plug still in or the trap blocked (and is it cleared now), or is the connection fine?
